summary: myCrop is a decision-support web app that helps farmers choose crop rotations that protect their soil, save water and adapt to a changing climate. For any farm location, it pulls 30 years of NASA POWER daily climate data (rainfall, temperature, solar radiation, humidity, wind) and turns it into a simple field report: drought, heat, frost and water-need risks shown as traffic-light cards and explained in plain words. The farmer adds what only he knows – his soil, his previous crops and his priorities – and can compare three rotations side by side, each scored out of 10 with the reasons. A 3D farm game lets him practise climate risks (drought, heatwaves, storms, salinity) before they happen in the real field, and a chatbot, Ammi Salah, answers in Arabic, Algerian Darja or English using only 15 verified scientific sources (FAO-56, FAO-66 and peer-reviewed crop research) and refuses to guess. It matters because small farmers rarely get access to satellite data in a form they can act on; myCrop brings NASA Earth observations to their own field.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

myCrop answers one question for a farmer: "Which crops should I grow next, in which order, on my field, with the climate I really have?"

1. Field report from NASA data – The farmer picks his farm on a map. The app downloads 30 years of NASA POWER daily data for that point and computes rainfall, reference evapotranspiration (FAO-56 Penman-Monteith), heat-stress days, frost days, dry spells and long-term trends (Mann-Kendall test, Theil-Sen slope). The result is shown as 6 simple traffic-light cards, with a detailed data view for experts.

2. Compare 3 rotations – The farmer chooses up to three rotations. Our engine evaluates each one against his real seasons (crop water needs, yield response to water stress, heat and frost at flowering, salinity tolerance, soil-health effects of legumes and residues) and gives each a score out of 10, explaining why one is better.

3. Local knowledge – The farmer enters his soil, irrigation, previous crops and priorities (water, income, soil health). These change the score, so the advice is personal.

4. Crop characteristics – Each crop card shows its water needs, root depth, sensitive stages and tolerances, taken from verified research.

5. 3D farm game – 12 levels, each a climate challenge built from real NASA seasons (drought, heatwave, storm, salinity…). Farmers practise decisions safely before they face them in the field.

6. Ammi Salah chatbot – Explains the farmer's own report, guides him through the app and answers crop questions in Arabic, Algerian Darja and English. Every answer cites one of 15 verified sources (FAO-56, FAO-66, Maas & Hoffman, Porter & Gawith, Angus et al., and others), and if the science does not answer the question, it says so instead of guessing.

HOW IT WORKS (TOOLS)

Front end: HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript; 3D game with WebGL. Back end: Python (data processing and statistics). Data: NASA POWER API (daily point data); if it cannot be reached, the app uses a cached copy on the phone, a pre-computed pack for all 58 Algerian wilayas, then ERA5 reanalysis (clearly labelled "not NASA"), so every region keeps working. Our cleaned dataset holds 87,664 values organised the same way for every farm.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Turns satellite data into decisions a farmer understands, in his own language.

- Helps save water, lower climate risk and rebuild soil health through better rotations.

- Works for any location NASA POWER covers, not only Algeria.

CREATIVITY

Storytelling through a farmer character (Kareem), a game that lets farmers "lose a harvest in the game instead of in the field", and a chatbot that refuses to guess.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Farmers with weak internet (fallback chain and offline cache), low digital literacy (simple words, traffic lights, voice-friendly chatbot), local languages (Darja), and trust (every number traceable to NASA data or a cited paper). We wrote 150 test cases covering different places and situations.
